blocks.orig: If you’ve ever seen either a gazelle or an antelope, you might be scratching your head, wondering how to tell the two apart, as, on a general inspection, you wouldn’t be blamed for thinking that they both look similar. Especially if they are a young calve or fawn – you’d be most likely to scratch your head and ask yourself, gazelle vs antelope – which one is it?
blocks.html: Anyone who has come across a gazelle or an antelope may well have paused and wondered which of the two they were looking at. At a quick glance the resemblance is strong, and nobody could hold it against you for mixing them up. That goes double when the animal is still a calf or fawn – you’d probably find yourself puzzling over the question, gazelle vs antelope – which is this?

blocks.orig: But we’re here to give you a definitive outline of each to avoid any future misunderstandings, and it will make you look good knowing you can point each one out.
blocks.html: That is where we come in: below you will find a clear description of each, so there is no confusion next time, and you will be able to impress your companions by naming them on sight.

blocks.orig: Read on to learn more about these two majestic-looking species.
blocks.html: Keep reading to find out more about these two graceful species.

blocks.orig: Put simply, all gazelles are antelopes, but not all antelopes are gazelles. More specifically, gazelle is a genus of antelope, so they are related in classification but less similar than an individual species.
blocks.html: In short: every gazelle is an antelope, yet not every antelope is a gazelle. To be more precise, gazelle is a genus within the antelopes, which means the two are linked in classification but not as closely as two individual species would be.

blocks.orig: You can identify these by their silky tan coats and display patterns of stripes and spots.
blocks.html: Gazelles are recognisable by their sleek tan coats, marked with patterns of stripes and spots.

blocks.orig: They also bear ring-shaped horns and are usually found in places such as Asia and China. Additionally, they can be found from the Horn of Africa, all the way to Tanzania.
blocks.html: Their horns are ringed, and they are typically found in regions such as Asia and China. Their range also stretches from the Horn of Africa right down to Tanzania.

blocks.orig: Their diet consists of plant leaves and stems, as they’re not as dependent on water as other species are.
blocks.html: Gazelles feed on the leaves and stems of plants, and they rely less on drinking water than other species do.

blocks.orig: These animals are also quite agile, so they can get out of a tight spot fast, as they are often prey to many predators such as cheetahs and even pythons. Gazelles have two toes encased in hooves, which is useful for when they need to bounce or slot out of danger.
blocks.html: They are also remarkably nimble, which lets them escape a tight spot in a hurry; after all, they are on the menu of many predators, from cheetahs to pythons. A gazelle has two hoofed toes on each foot, handy when it needs to bound or slot its way out of trouble.

blocks.orig: In comparison regarding gazelle vs antelope, the latter has even toes, smooth hair, and horns that are more straight-looking. Most male antelopes have horns, and so do only two-thirds of female antelopes.
blocks.html: Set against the gazelle, the antelope has even toes, smooth hair and horns that look straighter. Almost all male antelopes carry horns, whereas only about two-thirds of females do.

blocks.orig: These species have a larger body, but that does mean that they are not as quick as gazelles, but their diet differs slightly, as some species of antelopes like to feed on small birds, mammals, and insects.
blocks.html: Antelopes are bigger-bodied, which means they are not as fast as gazelles. Their diet is a little different too: certain antelope species will eat small birds, mammals and insects.

blocks.orig: During dry periods, where feed is below 40% moisture content, an antelope will drink around 2.8 liters of water a day, but this is only if they can’t find water through the consumption of things such as grass, leaves, or mulch.
blocks.html: In dry spells, when the feed they eat contains less than 40% moisture, an antelope drinks roughly 2.8 litres of water a day, though only when it cannot get enough moisture from grass, leaves, mulch and the like.

blocks.orig: You can often find specific types of antelope in various regions of Africa and Europe, and as there are 91 different species of antelope, we don’t blame you for not knowing the key features of each one. And sometimes, you might even find a unicorn 😉
blocks.html: Particular kinds of antelope turn up in different parts of Africa and Europe, and with 91 separate species of antelope in existence, we won't blame you for not knowing the defining features of each. Now and then you may even come across a unicorn 😉

blocks.orig: Now you have an idea of each species, it’s a good idea to talk about their similarities. These common characteristics between antelope vs gazelle might be why we often confuse the two. The main one, however, is that both are members of the bovid family, which is a broad category in and of itself.
blocks.html: With a picture of each species in mind, it makes sense to look at what they have in common. These shared traits between antelope vs gazelle are probably the reason the two get confused so often. The biggest one is that both belong to the bovid family, itself a very broad grouping.

blocks.orig: Both are usually considered herbivores, as some types of antelope, like the duiker, might divert from this description slightly as they can be considered omnivores. Still, this can be quite flexible, depending on the environment and the scarcity of certain sources.
blocks.html: Both are generally regarded as herbivores, although certain antelopes, the duiker for instance, stray from that description a little and can count as omnivores. Even that is fairly flexible, depending on the habitat and how scarce particular food sources are.

blocks.orig: One of the most notable similarities is that both types of bovid tend to travel in small to large groups, as some of these can have up to 700 members. However, antelopes can move in larger groups of thousands, which is more apparent when witnessing their annual migration.
blocks.html: Among the most striking similarities is that both kinds of bovid tend to move in groups, anything from small to large; some number up to 700 animals. Antelopes, though, can travel in far bigger herds of thousands, which is most obvious during their yearly migration.

blocks.orig: If you watch a gazelle averting danger, you’ll notice how they leap or slot to alert others in their group or use it to slip away from a predator, and you can also see this movement in action during mating season.
blocks.html: Watch a gazelle avoiding danger and you will see it leap or slot, either to warn the rest of its group or to give a predator the slip; the same movement is on display during the mating season.

blocks.orig: Interestingly, an antelope can inhabit a range of environments such as deserts, cold tundras, and areas by lakes and oceans, and some gazelles, like the Tibetan, live in high mountain meadows, as other species are more adapted to live in dry and desert environments.
blocks.html: It is interesting that antelopes can live in a wide range of environments, from deserts and cold tundra to the shores of lakes and oceans, while certain gazelles, such as the Tibetan gazelle, inhabit high mountain meadows and other species are better suited to arid and desert conditions.
